cues.text: A Chair Given Up for the Missions
Born on the island of Majorca in 1713 and baptized Miguel José, the future Junípero Serra entered the Franciscan order at sixteen.
He earned a doctorate in theology and held the prestigious Duns Scotus chair of philosophy at the Lullian University in Palma.
At thirty-five, he set aside this comfortable, respected academic career to join the missionary college of San Fernando in Mexico City, sailing for the New World in 1749.
His decision stunned colleagues who had assumed the brilliant young professor was destined for a lifetime of academic distinction rather than the hardship of missionary life in an unmapped land.
A Wound That Never Healed
Traveling on foot from Veracruz to Mexico City soon after his arrival, Serra suffered a leg injury that left him in chronic pain for the remainder of his life.

Rather than favor the injury, Serra insisted on continuing his missionary journeys largely on foot whenever the terrain allowed, treating the affliction as simply one more small penance offered alongside his larger missionary labor.
He would carry this pain quietly for the rest of his life, rarely mentioning it even to his closest companions.
Nine Years Among the Sierra Gorda
Serra spent his first nine years in the New World serving the Pame Indian missions of the Sierra Gorda north of Querétaro.

He learned the native language well enough to translate the catechism into it—foundational years of patient linguistic and pastoral labor that prepared him for the far larger missionary undertaking still ahead.
Founding the California Missions
In 1767, when the Spanish crown expelled the Jesuits from its territories, Franciscan friars under Serra's leadership were assigned to take over Baja California's missions.
The following year, already in his mid-fifties, Serra led an expedition northward into largely unmapped Alta California .
He founded Mission San Diego in 1769, the first of nine missions he would personally establish along the California coast over the following fifteen years.
Together, they anchored a chain of settlements that would eventually give many of California's largest modern cities their names and original sites.
Along the way he also helped establish the presidio at Santa Barbara and worked tirelessly to secure fair treatment for the native converts under his spiritual charge.
A Legacy Still Genuinely Debated

Serra's missionary methods and the broader consequences of the California mission system for the indigenous peoples it encountered remain subjects of serious and legitimate historical debate to this day.
Modern historians carefully weigh the missions' record of forced labor, corporal punishment, and introduced disease's devastating impact on native populations.
They consider this alongside Serra's own recorded advocacy on behalf of indigenous converts against harsh treatment by Spanish soldiers.
This complexity is worth holding squarely rather than smoothing over in either direction.
Legacy

Serra died at Mission San Carlos Borromeo in Carmel on 28 August 1784, having personally confirmed and baptized thousands of native converts across a missionary career that spanned, in all, thirty-five years.
Beatified in 1988 and canonized by Pope Francis in 2015, Serra remains honored as the Apostle of California.
His canonization was the first ceremony ever held on American soil.
A small, limping friar, his religious foundations, whatever the full complexity of their legacy, permanently shaped the geography, names, and Catholic identity of an entire American state.
